questions.q:
In a saturated solution of the sparingly soluble electrolyte ${AgIO}_{3}$~(molecular mass$= 283$), the equilibrium which sets in is~${AgIO}_{3} \left(s\right) ⇌ {Ag}_{}^{+} \left($aq\right) + ${IO}_{3}^{-}\left($aq\right)$.
If the solubility product constant ${K}_{sp}$ of ${AgIO}_{3}$ at a given temperature is $1 . 0 $\times {10}^{- 8},what is the mass of ${AgIO}_{3}$~in $100mL$ of its saturated solution?$
questions.solution:
$\begin{cases}{AgIO}_{3} & ⇌ & {Ag}^{+}\left(aq\right) & + & {IO}_{3}^{-}\left(aq\right) \\ S & S\end{cases}$
So,~${K}_{sp} = S^{2}$,

or~$S^{2} = 1 . 0 \times {10}^{- 8}$,

or~$S = 1 . 0 \times {10}^{- 4}molL^{- 1}$

$= 1 . 0 \times {10}^{- 4} \times 283gL^{- 1}$,

$= \dfrac{1\text{.}0 \times 1{0}^{- 4} \times \text{283}}{1000}{g mL}^{- 1}$,

$= \dfrac{1\text{.}0 \times 1{0}^{- 4} \times \text{283} \times \text{100}}{1000}\dfrac{g}{100 mL}$,

$= 28 . 3 \times {10}^{- 4}\dfrac{g}{100mL}$,

$= 2 . 83 \times {10}^{- 3}\dfrac{g}{100mL}$.

questions.q:
In an aqueous solution, the ionization constants for carbonic acid are

${K}_{1} = \text{4.2} \times 1 {0}^{- 7}$ and ${~K}_{2} = \text{4.8} \times 1 {0}^{- 11}$

Select the correct statement for a saturated $\text{0.034 M}$ solution of the carbonic acid:
options: The concentration of $H^{+}$ is double that of ${CO}_{3}^{2 -}$.
The concentration of ${CO}_{3}^{2 -}$ is greater than that of ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$.
The concentration of $H^{+}$ and ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$ are approximately equal.
questions.solution:
$\begin{cases}{H}_{2} {CO}_{3} & ⇌ & H^{+} & + & {HCO}_{3}^{-} \text{;} & {K}_{1} & = & \text{4.2} \times 1 {0}^{- 7} \\ {HCO}_{3}^{-} & ⇌ & H^{+} & + & {CO}_{3}^{2 -} \text{;} & {K}_{2} & = & \text{4.8} \times 1 {0}^{- 1 1}\end{cases}$

$∵ {K}_{1} ≫ {K}_{2}$, so ${H}_{2} {CO}_{3}$ ionises more than ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$ and hence, contribution of $H^{+}$ is mostly due to ionization of carbonic acid. Thus, the concentrations of $H^{+}$ and ${HCO}_{3}^{-}$ are approximately equal.

questions.solution: Given, Ionic product of $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2=5.5 \times 10^{-6}$ Concentration of $\mathrm{NaOH}$ solution $=0.10 \mathrm{M}\because$ Ionic product of $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2=5.5 \times 10^{-6}$ or, $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2= \left[\mathrm{Ca}^{2+}\right]+2 \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right] Let, solubility $=S\$begin{gathered}\m$mathrm{Ca}^{2+}+2 \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]\\ S \quad(2 S)^2\end{gathered}$ Also, $K_{\mathrm{sp}}=4 S^3$ where, $K_{\mathrm{sp}}=$ solubility product $\therefore$ Due to common ion effect, Molar solubility of $\mathrm{Ca}(\mathrm{OH})_2=\frac{5.5 \times 10^{-6}}{0.1 \times 0.1}=5.5 \times10^{-4}$

questions.q: The successive equilibrium constants for the stepwise dissociation of a tribasic acid are $K_1$, $K_2$ and $K_3$, respectively. The equilibrium constant for the overall dissociation is
questions.solution:
For a tribasic acid like $\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4$ has three ionisation constant. The overall ionisation constants $(K)$ will be product of ionisation constants of three steps, i.e. K=K_1 \times K_2 \times K_3 $\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4 \rightleftharpoons \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{PO}_4^{-}$
$\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{PO}_4^{-} \rightleftharpoons \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrm{HPO}_4^{2-}$
$\mathrm{HPO}_4^{2-} \rightleftharpoons \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-}$
Adding Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get $\begin{gathered} \mathrm{H}}_{3} \mathrm{PO}_4 \rightleftharpoons 3 \mathrmH^{+}+\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-} \\ $K=\frac{\left[\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-}\right]\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]^3}{\left[\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4\right]} \end{gathered}$Multiply mathematical Eqs. (i), (ii) and (iii), we get $\begin{gathered}$K_1 \times K_2 \times $K_3=\frac{\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{PO}_4^{-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4\right]} \times \frac{\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{HPO}_4^{2-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{PO}_4^{-}\right]}$\\ \times $\frac{\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]\left[\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{HPO}_4^{2-}\right]}$\\ K_1 K_2 $K_3=\frac{\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]^3\left[\mathrm{PO}_4^{3-}\right]}{\left[\mathrm{H}_3 \mathrm{PO}_4\right]} \end{gathered}$Overall ionisation constant $K, K=K_1 \times K_2 \times K_3

questions.q: $\mathrm{pH}$ of a buffer solution decreases by 0.02 units when $0.12 \mathrm{~g}$ of acetic acid is added to $250 \mathrm{~mL}$ of a buffer solution of acetic acid and potassium acetate at $27^{{}^{{}^{\circ}}} \mathrm{C}$. The buffer capacity of the solution is
questions.solution:
Buffer capacity, $\beta=\frac{d C_{\mathrm{HA}}}{d_{\mathrm{pH}}}$,
where, $d C_{\mathrm{HA}}=$ no. of moles of acid added per litre
$\begin{aligned}
d_{\mathrm{pH}} & =\text { change in } \mathrm{pH} \\
d C_{\mathrm{HA}} & =\frac{\text { moles of acetic acid }}{\text { volume }} \\
& =\frac{0.12 / 60}{250 / 1000}=\frac{1}{125} \\
\therefore \quad \beta & =\frac{1 / 125}{0.02}=\frac{1}{2.5}=0.4
\end{aligned}$

questions.q:
The minimum conc. of NH4Cl required to prevent the precipitation of Mg(OH)2 from a solution of 0.05 M Mg2+ and 0.05 M NH3 is x 10-3. What is the value of x in nearest whole number ?

(Ksp( Mg(OH)2) = 9.0 x 10-12 , Kb (NH4OH) = 1.8 x 10-5)
questions.solution:
$Conc. of \left[{OH}^{-}\right] = \sqrt{\dfrac{{K}_{sp}}{\left({Mg}^{2 +}\right)}} = \text{1.34} × 1 {0}^{- 5}$

${K}_{{NH}_{4} \text{OH}} = \dfrac{\left[{NH}_{4}^{+}\right] \left[\text{1.34} × 1 {0}^{- 5}\right]}{\text{0.05}}$

\left[{NH}_{4}^{+}\right] = \text{0.0671 M} = \text{67.1} × 1 {0}^{- 3} M$

So, answer is 67.

Alternative solution

IF Mg(OH)2(s) is just formed then the equilibria existing are

$\begin{cases}\text{Mg} {\left(\text{OH}\right)}_{2 \left(\text{s}\right)} + \text{Aq.} & ⇌ & {Mg}^{2 +} + 2 {OH}_{\text{aq}}^{-} & \text{;} & {K}_{sp} \\ 2 {OH}_{\text{aq}}^{-} + 2 {NH}_{4 \left(\text{aq}\right)}^{+} & ⇌ & 2 {NH}_{3} + 2 {H}_{2} \text{O} & \text{;} & \dfrac{1}{{K}_b^{2}}\end{cases}$

$\begin{cases}\text{Mg} {\left(\text{OH}\right)}_{2 \left(\text{s}\right)} + 2 {NH}_{4 \left(\text{aq}\right)}^{+} & ⇌ & {Mg}^{2 +} + 2 {NH}_{3} + 2 {H}_{2} \text{O}\text{;} & \text{;} & {K}_{eq} = \dfrac{{K}_{sp}}{{K}_b^{2}}\end{cases}$

${K}_{eq} = \dfrac{9 × 1 {0}^{- 1 2}}{{\left(\text{1.8} × 1 {0}^{- 5}\right)}^{2}} = \dfrac{\left[{Mg}^{2 +}\right] {\left[{NH}_{3}\right]}^{2}}{{\left[{NH}_{4}^{+}\right]}^{2}}$

${\left[{NH}_{4}^{+}\right]}^{2} = \dfrac{\left[{Mg}^{2 +}\right] {\left[{NH}_{3}\right]}^{2}}{9 × 1 {0}^{- 1 2}} × {\left(\text{1.8} × 1 {0}^{- 5}\right)}^{2}$

$= \dfrac{5 × 1 {0}^{- 2} × {\left(5 × 1 {0}^{- 2}\right)}^{2} × {\left(\text{1.8} × 1 {0}^{- 5}\right)}^{2}}{9 × 1 {0}^{- 1 2}}$

$= \dfrac{1 2 5 × \text{3.24} × 1 {0}^{- 1 6}}{9 × 1 {0}^{- 1 2}} = 4 5 × 1 {0}^{- 4}$

\left[{NH}_{4}^{+}\right] = \text{6.70} × 1 {0}^{- 2} = 6 7 × 1 {0}^{- 3}$

$\text{x} = 6 7$

questions.q: $75 \mathrm{~mL}$ of $0.2 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{HCl}$ is mixed with $25 \mathrm{~mL}$ of $1 \mathrm{M}\mathrm{HCl}$. To this solution, $300 \mathrm{~mL}$ of distilled water is added. What is the $\mathrm{pH}$ of the resultant solution?
questions.solution:
$\begin{aligned}$V_1 & =75 $\mathrm{~mL},$V_2=25 $\mathrm{~mL}$\\
M_1 & =0.2 $\mathrm{M},$M_2=1 $\mathrm{M}$\\
V_3 & =300 $\mathrm{~mL}, \mathrm{pH}=$? \\
V & =V_1+V_2=75+25=100 $\mathrm{~mL}$\\
M & =$\frac{V_1 M_1+V_2 M_2}{V_1+V_2}=\frac{75 \times 0.2 \times 25+1}{75+25}=$0.4 $\mathrm{M}
\end{aligned}\therefore$ Total volume $\begin{aligned}$V^{\prime}=V_1+V_2+V_3 & =75+25+300=400 $\mathrm{~mL}$\\
M V & =M^{\prime} V^{\prime} \\
0.4 $\times$100 & =M^{\prime} $\times$400 \\
M & =0.1 $\mathrm{M}
\end{aligned} \text { Concentration of } \mathrm{HCl}=$0.1=10^{-1} \therefore \quad $\mathrm{pH}=-\log _{10}\left[\mathrmH^{+}\right]=$1

questions.q: At \(T($\mathrm{~K})$\), if the ionisation constant of ammonia in solution is \(2.5 $\times$10^{-5}\), the \($\mathrm{pH}$\) of \(0.01 $\mathrm{M}$\) ammonia solution and the ionisation constant of its conjugate acid respectively at that temperature are \((\log 2=0.30)\)
questions.solution: \(K_a \times K_b=K_w=10^{-14}\) (at \(25^{\circ} $\mathrm{C}$\)) where, \(K_a=\) ionisation constant for acid \$(\left(\mathrm{NH}}_{4}^{+}\right)\) and \(K_b=\) ionisation constant for base \$(\left(\mathrm{NH}}_{3}\right)\) \(=2.5 \times 10^{-5}\) i.e. \(\quad $K_a\left(\mathrm{NH}}_{4}^{+}\right) \cdot $K_b\left(\mathrm{NH}}_{3}\right)=10^{-14}\) \(\begin{gathered} \therefore \quad $K_a\left(\mathrm{NH}}_{4}^{+}\$right)=\frac{10^{-14}}{K_a\left(\mathrm{NH}_4^{+}\right)}$\\ $K_a=\frac{10^{-14}}{2.5 \times 10^{-5}}=$4 \times 10^{-10} \end{gathered}\) i.e. ionisation constant of conjugate acid \(=4 \times 10^{-8}\) For \$(\mathrm{pH}$\) of \(0.01 $\mathrm{M}$\) ammonia \$(\left(\mathrm{NH}}_{3}\right)\) \(\therefore $\mathrm{NH}}_{4} $\mathrm{OH}$\) dissociate as : \(\begin{array}{llll} & $\mathrm{NH}}_{4} $\mathrm{OH} \rightleftharpoons$& $\mathrm{NH}}_{4}^{+} \text{ and } $+\mathrm{OH}^{-}$\\ $\text {At equilibrium }$ \text{ and } 0.01 (1-\alpha) \text{ and } 0. \alpha \text{ and } 0.01 \alpha\end{array}\) (\(\therefore\) Concentration of ammonia solution \(=0.01 $\mathrm{M}$\)) Also, \(\$alpha=\sqrt{\frac{K_b}{C}}=\sqrt{\frac{2.5 \times 10^{-5}}{0.01}}=$0.05\) and \$(\left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=\mathrm{C} \alpha=($0.01) \alpha\) or \$(  \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]=$0.0005\) \(\therefore \quad $\mathrm{pOH}=-\log \left[\mathrm{OH}^{-}\right]$\) or, \$(\m$mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH}=$14+\log [(0.01) \alpha]=14-3.3\) Thus, \$(\mathrm{pH}=$10.7\) and also ionisation constant \$(\left($K_a\right)=4 \times 10^{-10}\)$

questions.q: What is the $\mathrm{pH}$ of $10 \mathrm{~L}$ of a buffer solution containing $0.01 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{Cl}$ and $0.1 \mathrm{M} \mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{OH}$ having $\mathrm{p} K_b$ of 5 ?
questions.solution: Given, concentration of salt \left(\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{Cl}\right)=0.01 \mathrm{M}$ Concentration of base \left(\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{OH}\right)=0.1 \mathrm{M}\mathrm{p} K_b=5$ A mixture of $\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{OH}$ and $\mathrm{NH}_4 \mathrm{Cl}$ forms basic buffer solution. The Henderson's equation for a basic buffer solution is $\mathrm{pOH}=\mathrm{p} K_b+\log \frac{[\text { Salt }]}{[\text { Base }]}\mathrm{p} K_b=-\log K_b=-\log 0.1=1$ By substituting values in the above equation, we get $\mathrm{pOH}=5+\log \frac{0.01}{0.1}=4\mathrm{pH}=14-\mathrm{pOH}=14-4=10$

questions.q: The solubility products of $\mathrm{NiS}, \mathrm{ZnS}, \mathrm{CdS}$ and $\mathrm{HgS}$ are $4.7 \times 10^{-5}, 1.6 \times 10^{-24}, 8 \times 10^{-27}$ and $4 \times 10^{-53}$ respectively. An aqueous solution contains $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}, \mathrm{Zn}^{2+}, \mathrm{Cd}^{2+}$ and $\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}$ of equal concentration. $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}$ gas was passed into this solution very slowly. The first and the last ions that precipitate as sulphides are respectively.
questions.solution: $\begin{aligned}$& $K_{\mathrm{sp}} $\text { of } \mathrm{NiS}=$4.7 $\times$10^{-5} \\  \text{ and }  $K_{\mathrm{sp}} $\text { of } \mathrm{ZnS}=$1.6 $\times$10^{-24} \\ & $K_{\mathrm{sp}} $\text { of } \mathrm{CdS}=$8 $\times$10^{-27} \\  \text{ and }  $K_{\mathrm{sp}} $\text { of } \mathrm{HgS}=$4 $\times$10^{-53} \end{aligned} Since, the solubility products of NiS is highest and that of $\mathrm{HgS}$ is lowest, it implies that $\mathrm{Hg}^{2+}$ will start precipitating quickly than any other salt on introduction of $\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{~S}$ (sulphide ion source). On the same account $\mathrm{Ni}^{2+}$ will precipitate last.

questions.q: Calculate the molar ratio of a weak acid \($\mathrm{H}$A\left($K_a=10^{-6}\right)\) and its salt with strong base, so that the \($\mathrm{pH}$\) of buffer solution is 6 .$
questions.solution: \(\begin{aligned} & $\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{pK}+\log \frac{[\text { Salt }]}{[\text { Acid }]} \log \frac{[\text { Salt }]}{[\text { Acid }]}$\\ & $=\frac{\mathrm{pH}}{\mathrm{p} K_a}=\frac{6}{6}=$1 \\ & ${\left[K_a=10^{-6} \therefore \mathrm{p} K_a=-\log K_a=\log \left(10^{-6}\right) \Rightarrow 6\right]}$\\ & \log $\frac{[\text { Salt }]}{[\text { Acid }]}=$1 \\ & $\frac{[\text { Acid }]}{[\text { Salt }]}=$10^{-1} $\text { or }$0.1 \end{aligned}\) Hence, the correct option is (d).

questions.q: An aqueous solution of $6 . 3gram$~oxalic acid dihydrate is made up to $250mL$. The volume of $0 . 1NNaOH$ required to completely neutralize $10milliLiter$ of this solution is:
questions.solution:
We know that the molecular formula of oxalic acid dihydrate is& $( COOH{)}_{2} . 2{H}_{2}O$.

As the n-factor of oxalic acid is~$2$, the total equivalents of oxalic acid in~$250ml = 2 ( \dfrac{6 . 3}{126} ) = \dfrac{1}{10}$

Therefore, the total equivalents of oxalic acid dihydrate in~$10ml = \dfrac{1}{10} \times \dfrac{1}{250} \times 10$

As~$0 . 1NofNaOH$,~having volume~$V$~is required to neutralize~$\dfrac{1}{250}$~equivalents of oxalic acid dihydrate, so,

$( 0 . 1 ) V = \dfrac{1}{250} ⇒ V = \dfrac{1}{25}l = \dfrac{1}{250} \times 1000ml ⇒ V = 40ml$&

questions.solution: $\mathrm{NaCN}$ is the salt of strong base $(\mathrm{NaOH})$ and weak acid (HCN). So, its $\mathrm{pH}>7$. $\mathrm{CuSO}_4$ is a salt of strong acid  \left(\mathrm{H}_2 \mathrm{SO}_4\right)$ and a weak base \left[\mathrm{Cu}(\mathrm{OH})_2\right.$, thus its solution is acidic with $\mathrm{pH} < 7$. $\mathrm{KCl}$ is a salt of strong acid $(\mathrm{HCl})$ and a strong base $[\mathrm{KOH}]$, thus its solution is neutral with $\mathrm{pH}=7$. Increasing order of $\mathrm{pH}$ is $\begin{array}{ccc} \mathrm{CuSO}}_{4} & < \mathrm{KCl} & < \mathrm{NaCN} \\ \text { I } & \text { III } & \text { II } \end{array} $

questions.q:
$Mg\left(OH\right)2$ is precipitated when $NaOH$ is added to a solution of ${Mg}^{2 +}$. If the final concentration of ${Mg}^{2 +}$ is ${10}^{- 10}M$, the concentration of ${OH}^{-} \left(M\right)$ in the solution is

[Solubility product for $Mg\left(OH\right)2 = 5 . 6 \times {10}^{- 12}]

$
questions.solution:
In the saturated solution of sparingly soluble electrolyte,& the ionic product of ions is constant at constant& temperature and it is known a Solubility Product.

Here,

$Mg ( OH{)}_{2} \to \left[{Mg}^{2 +}\right]\left[{OH}^{-}\right]2$

Given,

${K}_{sp}$~for~$Mg ( OH{)}_{2} = 5 . 6 \times {10}^{- 12}$

\left[{Mg}^{2 +}\right] = {10}^{- 10}M$

Substituting the value, we get :

${K}_{sp} = \left[{Mg}^{2 +}\right]\left[{OH}^{-}\right]2 ⇒ 5 . 6 \times {10}^{- 12} = \left[{10}^{- 10}\right]\left[{OH}^{-}\right]2 ⇒ {OH}^{-} = 0 . 24M$

Hence, the~concentration of~$[ {OH}^{-} ] = 0 . 24M$

$

questions.q: Acetic acid and propionic acid have ${K}_{a}$ values $1.75 \times 1{0}^{- 5}$ and $1.3 \times 1{0}^{- 5}$ respectively at a certain temperature. An equimolar solution of a mixture of the two acids is partially neutralised by NaOH. How is the ratio of the contents of acetate and propionate ions related to the ${K}_{a}$ values and the molarity?
options: \left(\dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha}\right) = \dfrac{1.75}{1.3} \times \left(\dfrac{\beta}{1 - \beta}\right)$ , whereas $\alpha$ and $\beta$ are ionized fractions of the acids$
The ratio is unrelated to the ${K}_{a}$ values
The ratio is unrelated to the molarity
The ratio is unrelated to the pH of the solution
questions.solution:
In a given mixture, the ionization of two acids can be written at
Let $\alpha, \beta$ be degree of ionization at same concentration.
$\mathop{C{H}_{3}COOH}_{1 - \alpha} ⇌ \mathop{C{H}_{3}COO^{-}}_{\alpha} + \mathop{H^{+}}_{\alpha + \beta}$
$\mathop{{C}_{2}{H}_{5}COOH}_{1 - \beta} ⇌ \mathop{{C}_{2}{H}_{5}COO^{-}}_{\beta} + \mathop{H^{+}}_{\alpha + \beta}$
So ${K}_{\text{Acetic}\text{acid}} \text{=}\dfrac{\left[\text{\alpha}\right]\left[\text{\alpha}\text{+}\text{\beta}\right] ⋅ \text{c}}{\left[\text{1} - \text{\alpha}\right]}$
${K}_{\text{Prepionic}\text{acid}} \text{=}\dfrac{\left[\text{\beta}\right]\left[\text{\alpha}\text{+}\text{\beta}\right] ⋅ \text{c}}{\left[\text{1} - \text{\beta}\right]}$
So $\dfrac{{K}_{\text{acetic}\text{acid}}}{{K}_{\text{propinoic}\text{acid}}} \text{=}\dfrac{α}{\text{1} - \text{\alpha}} \text{\times}\dfrac{\left(\text{1} - \text{\beta}\right)}{β}$
or \dfrac{\alpha}{1 - \alpha} = \dfrac{1.75}{1.3} \times \left[\dfrac{\beta}{1 - \beta}\right].

questions.q:
How much of 0.3 M $N{H}_{4}OH$ should be mixed with 30 mL of 0.2 M solution of $N{H}_{4}Cl$ to give buffer solution of pH 8.65?
(Given: ${\text{pK}}_{b}$ of ${\text{NH}}_{3} = 4.75$)
questions.solution:
It is a basic buffer
$pH = 8.65$ ,
pOH = 14 – 8.65 = 5.35
$pOH = p{K}_{b} + log\dfrac{[ \overset{⊕}{N}{H}_{4} ]}{[ N{H}_{4}OH ]}$
5.35 = 4.75 + log $\dfrac{[ \overset{⊕}{N}{H}_{4} ]}{[ N{H}_{4}OH ]}$
$\dfrac{[ \overset{⊕}{N}{H}_{4} ]}{[ N{H}_{4}OH ]} =$ antilog (5.35 – 4.75)
= antilog (0.6) $\approx 4.0$
So $\dfrac{[ \overset{⊕}{N}{H}_{4} ]}{[ N{H}_{4}OH ]} = \dfrac{30 \times 0.2}{0.3 \times V} \approx 4.0$
So V = 5 mL.

questions.q: The heats of neutralization of ${CH}_{3}COOH, HCOOH, HCN$and ${H}_{2}S$ are $- 13 . 2, - 13 . 4, - 2 . 9$ and $- 3 . 8kcal$ per equivalent respectively. The correct increasing order of acid strength is
questions.solution:
$\Delta {H}_{ionisation} = \left|\Delta {H}_{neutralisation}\right|\text{experimental} - \left|\Delta {H}_{neutral}\right|\text{theoretical}$

$\Delta {H}_{ionisation}\left({CH}_{3}\text{COOH}\right) = - \text{13.20} + \text{13.75} = \text{0.55}\text{kcal}{ mol}^{- 1}$

$\Delta {H}_{ionisation}\left(\text{HCOOH}\right) = - \text{13.40} + \text{13.75} = \text{0.35}\text{kcal}{ mol}^{- 1}$

$\Delta {H}_{ionisation}\left(\text{HCN}\right) = - \text{2.90} + \text{13.75} = \text{10.85}\text{kcal}{ mol}^{- 1}$

$\Delta {H}_{ionisation}\left({H}_{2}\text{S}\right) = - \text{3.80} + \text{13.75} = \text{9.95}\text{kcal}{ mol}^{- 1}$

$- 13 . 75kcal{mol}^{- 1}$ is the standard enthalpy of neutralisation for strong acid or a strong base. Higher the ionisation enthalpy,~weaker is the acid.


$HCN < {H}_{2}S < {CH}_{3}COOH < HCOOH$

questions.q:
${H}_{2}S$ is bubbled through $0 . 2MNaCN$ solution which is $0 . 02M$~in each $\text{Ag}{\text{CN}}_{2 ( \text{aq)}}^{- 1}$ and $\text{Cd}{\text{CN}}_{4 ( \text{aq)}}^{2 -}$.~ Determine which sulphide will precipitate first.

${K}_{sp} \left({Ag}_{2} \text{S}\right) = 1 {0}^{- 5 0} \text{,} { K}_{sp} \left(\text{CdS}\right) = 7 \times 1 {0}^{- 2 8}$

${K}_{f} \text{Ag} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{2}^{- 1} = 2 \text{.} 5 \times 1 {0}^{2 0} \text{,} { K}_{f} \text{Cd} { \left(\text{CN}\right)}_{4 \text{aq}}^{2 -} = 1 {0}^{1 7}$.

\left[S^{2 -}\right]$ ion concentration for ${Ag}_{2}S$ and $CdS$ may be reported as:$
questions.solution:
$\begin{cases}2Ag{CN}_{2aq}^{- 1} & ⇌ & 2{Ag}_{aq}^{+} + 4{CN}_{aq}^{- 1} & ; & \dfrac{1}{{K}_{f}2\left({AgCN}_{2}\right)- 1} \\ 2{Ag}^{+} + {S}_{aq}^{2 -} & ⇌ & {Ag}_{2}S\left(s\right) & ; & \dfrac{1}{{K}_{sp}\left({Ag}_{2}S\right)}\end{cases}$
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
$\begin{cases}2 \text{Ag} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{2 \text{aq}}^{- 1} + {S}_{aq}^{2 -} & ⇌ & {Ag}_{2} \text{S} \left(\text{s}\right) + 4 {CN}_{aq}^{- 1} & \text{;} & \dfrac{1}{{K}_{\text{sp} \left({Ag}_{2} \text{s}\right)} {K}_f^{2} \left(\text{Ag} {CN}_{2}^{- 1}\right)} = {K}_{1}\end{cases}$

${K}_{1} = \dfrac{1 {0}^{+ 5 0}}{6 \text{.} 2 5 \times 1 {0}^{4 0}} = 1 \text{.} 6 \times 1 {0}^{9}    {K}_{1} = \dfrac{1}{{K}_{\text{sp} {Ag}_{2} \text{S}} \cdot   {K}_f^{2 } \left(\text{Ag} {CN}_{2}^{- 1}\right)}$

$1 \text{.} 6 \times 1 {0}^{9} = \dfrac{{\left[{CN}^{- 1}\right]}^{4}}{{\left[\text{Ag} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{2}^{- 1}\right]}^{2} \left[S^{2 -}\right]} = \dfrac{{\left(0 \text{.} 2\right)}^{4}}{{\left(0 \text{.} 0 2\right)}^{2 } \left[S^{2 -}\right]}$

$∴\left[S^{2 -}\right] = 2 \text{.} 5 \times 1 {0}^{- 9} \text{M}$~ for precipitation of ${Ag}_{2}S$.

$\begin{cases}\text{Cd} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{4 \text{aq}}^{- 2} & ⇌ & {Cd}^{2 +} + 4 {CN}_{aq}^{- 1} & \text{;} & \dfrac{1}{{K}_{f} \text{Cd} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{4}^{2 -}} \\ {Cd}_{aq}^{2 +} + {S}_{aq}^{2 -} & ⇌ & \text{Cd} \text{S} \left(\text{S}\right) & \text{;} & \dfrac{1}{{K}_{sp} \left(\text{Cd} \text{S}\right)}\end{cases}$
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
$\begin{cases}\text{Cd} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{4 \text{aq}}^{2 -} & + {S}_{\text{aq}}^{2 -} & ⇌ & 4 {CN}_{aq}^{- 1} + \text{Cd} \text{S} \left(\text{s}\right) & \text{;}\end{cases} {   K}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{{K}_{sp} \left(\text{CdS}\right) \cdot {  K}_{f} \text{Cd} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{4}^{2 -}}$

${K}_{2} = \dfrac{1}{7 \times 1 {0}^{- 2 8}} \times \dfrac{1}{1 {0}^{1 7}} = 1 \text{.} 4 2 8 \times 1 {0}^{1 0}$

$1 \text{.} 4 2 8 \times 1 {0}^{1 0} = \dfrac{{\left[{CN}^{- 1}\right]}^{4}}{{\left[\text{Cd} {\left(\text{CN}\right)}_{4}\right]}^{2 -} \left[S^{2 -}\right]} = \dfrac{{\left(0 \text{.} 2\right)}^{4}}{\left(0 \text{.} 0 2\right) \left[S^{2 -}\right]}$

\left[S^{2 -}\right] = 5 \text{.} 6 \times 1 {0}^{- 1 2}$~ required for precipitation of $CdS$.

Lower sulphide ion concentration needed for $CdS$, so, \text{ and } it will precipitate out first.$

questions.q: A certain weak acid has a dissociation constant of $\text{1.0} \times 1 {0}^{- 4}$ . The equilibrium constant for its reaction with a strong base is :

$\text{HX} ⇌ H^{+} + X^{-}$

${K}_{a} = 1 {0}^{- 4} = \dfrac{\left[H^{+}\right] \left[X^{-}\right]}{\left[\text{HX}\right]} .....(i)$

$\text{HX} + \text{NaOH} ⇌ \text{NaX} + {H}_{2} \text{O}$

${K}_{eq} = \dfrac{\left[{Na}^{+}\right] \left[X^{-}\right]}{\left[\text{HX}\right] \left[{Na}^{+}\right] \left[{OH}^{-}\right]} = \dfrac{\left[X^{-}\right]}{\left[\text{HX}\right] \left[{OH}^{-}\right]} .....(ii)$

By Eqns. (i) and (ii)

$\dfrac{{K}_{eq}}{{K}_{a}} = \dfrac{1}{{K}_{w}}∴ {K}_{eq} = \dfrac{{K}_{a}}{{K}_{w}} = \dfrac{1 {0}^{- 4}}{1 {0}^{- 1 4}} = 1 {0}^{1 0}$

questions.q: $MY$ and $N{Y}_{3}$, two nearly insoluble salts, have the same ${K}_{sp}$~of~$6.2 \times {10}^{- 13}$ at room temperature. Which of the following statement is~true with respect to~$MY$ and $N{Y}_{3}$?
options: The molar solubilities of $MY$ and $N{Y}_{3}$ in water are identical.
The molar solubility of $MY$ in water is less than that of the molar solubility of~$N{Y}_{3}$ .
The salts $MY$ and $N{Y}_{3}$ are soluble~more in $0 . 5MKY$ than& the pure water.
The addition of salt $KY$ to the solution of $MY$ and $N{Y}_{3}$ does& not& have any effect on their solubilities.
questions.solution:
For& $MY$,~an insoluble salt,

${K}_{sp} = s^{2}$

$MY \left(s\right) ⇌ M^{+} \left($aq\right) + $Y^{-}\left($aq\right)$

For~$N{Y}_{3}$,~an~insoluble salt,

${K}_{sp} = 4s^{3}$

$N{Y}_{3} \left($s\right) ⇌ N^{+} \left($aq\right) + $3Y^{-}\left($aq\right)$

$∴ $S\left($MY\right) = $\sqrt{6 . 2 \times {10}^{- 13}} =$7 . 8 $\times {10}^{- 7}

$∴ $S\left($N{Y}_{3}\right) = $\$left(\dfrac{6 . 2 \times {10}^{- 13}}{4}\right)\dfrac{1}{3} =5 . 2 $\times {10}^{- 5}

$∴ S \left($MY\right) < S \left($N{Y}_{3}\right)

$

questions.q:
Which of the following equations give ionic product of water?

(i) ${NH}_{3\left(aq\right)} + {H}_{2}O ⇆ {NH}_{4\left(aq\right)}^{+} + {OH}_{aq}^{-}$

(ii) ${NH}_{4\left(aq\right)}^{+} + {H}_{2}O ⇆ {H}_{3}O^{+} + {NH}_{3\left(aq\right)}$

(iii) ${NH}_{2\left(aq\right)}^{-} + {H}_{2}O ⇆ {NH}_{3\left(aq\right)} + {OH}^{-}$

(iv) ${NH}_{3\left(aq\right)} + {OH}_{aq}^{-} ⇆ {NH}_{2\left(aq\right)}^{-} + {H}_{2}O$
questions.solution:
The equation of the ionic product of water can be written as:

${H}_{2}O ⇌ H^{+} + {OH}^{-}or, 2{H}_{2}O ⇌ {H}_{3}O^{+} + {OH}^{-}$

The above equation can be obtained by adding the first two given equations:

$\dfrac{{NH}_{3\left(aq\right)} + {H}_{2}O ⇆ {NH}_{4\left(aq\right)}^{+} + {OH}_{aq}^{-}{NH}_{4\left(aq\right)}^{+} + {H}_{2}O ⇆ {H}_{3}O^{+} + {NH}_{3\left(aq\right)}}{2{H}_{2}O ⇌ {H}_{3}O^{+} + {OH}^{-}}$

Hence, on doing basic manipulations in~ \left(i\right) \text{ and } \left(ii\right)$& we are able to get required equation for ionic product of water

$
